newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Opposition plans final attack on Kabul in days.
newsitem.headline: Opposition plans final attack on Kabul in days.

text.p: An Afghan opposition alliance threatening to take Kabul has lost patience with peace efforts and plans a final attack on Afghanistan's capital within days, a spokesman for the group said on Tuesday.
The spokesman also dismissed as "wishful thinking" reports by Afghanistan's Taleban administration in Kabul of splits in the alliance of northern Afghan Uzbeks, Tajiks and Hazaras.
The Taleban, who captured Kabul last September, are an alliance of southern Afghanistan's Pashtuns, the majority group in the country.

Here in this dusty northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif, rear headquarters of the so-called Northern Alliance, there is none of the tension and fear that grip Kabul, which for the past week has come under rocket and air attack from approaching alliance forces.
Trucks laden with melons, the only luxury at this time of the year when temperatures soar to 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit), disgorge their cargoes at street markets which seem full of goods.
Alliance warplanes as well as transport aircraft regularly take off from the airfield. Helicopters also fly to the war's front line.

There are few signs of excessive security except at key military installations. There are no patrols on city streets, unlike in Kabul where there have been reports of roundups of opponents of the Taleban and forced drafting of young men into military service.
"There is a real mood of confidence and optimism about what is going to happen in the battle for Kabul," a foreign aid worker said in Mazar-i-Sharif.

The alliance spokesman, a former Afghan Foreign Ministry official who identified himself only as Chief Protocol Officer Zia, said the group's forces were within 13 km (eight miles) of the outskirts of Kabul and had the capital in a stranglehold.
He said the only reason a final push had not yet started was that rear supply lines were being secured.
"The final battle will start within days," Zia told a small group of foreign reporters.

Asked if there was a chance of a last-ditch peace effort to avoid a bloody street battle for Kabul, Zia replied: "What would be the point? We are ready for negotiations but each time conditions are put on starting them. We have run out of patience."
He said diplomatic initiatives by Pakistan, Iran and the United Nations were at an end and had nowhere to go.
"We have no word of anyone coming here in the near future so we will end this stalemate ourselves," Zia said. "We will take Kabul."

U.N. special envoy for Afghanistan Norbert Holl is due to leave Pakistan for Mazar-i-Sharif on Saturday while a Pakistani emissary is planning to visit here after talks with Taleban officials in the southern town of Kandahar on Wednesday.

In a sign of how an almost de facto partition of Afghanistan has taken place into a southern part run by the Taleban and a northern part run by the alliance, officials here dismiss visas issued by Afghan embassies abroad if the authority is the Taleban government.

"These visas do not count," a Mazar-i-Sharif airport official told foreign journalists who had visa stamps from the Afghan embassy in Islamabad. "We will issue you our visas," he said as passports were stamped.

The main players in the northern alliance, which has less fundamentalist Islamic views of how the country should be run than the Taleban, are Ahmad Shah Masood, a hero of the battle against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan in the 1980s, and a 37-year old Russian army-trained general, Abdul Malik, an Uzbek.

Masood is the front-line commander of the alliance forces while Malik, based in Mazar-i-Sharif, has the greatest number of forces, estimated to number at least 10,000 backed by tanks, helicopters and the planes that have been bombing Kabul.
Masood is a former defence minister and the main military commander of the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.

In May, Malik led a mutiny against former northern warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum forcing him to flee to Turkey, and struck a deal with the Taleban allowing the purist Islamic militia to take Mazar-i-Sharif.
But within days, forces led by Malik and the Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction turned on the Taleban and drove them from Mazar-i-Sharif after heavy street battles.
"General Malik and General Masood speak several times a day on the radio coordinating our plans," Zia said in dismissing reports of a split between the two.

In a possible sign that Malik is fully involved this week in war preparations, he cancelled an appointment on Monday with U.N. human rights monitors who visited the city to prepare their annual report on Afghanistan ahead of this year's U.N. General Assembly. The monitors instead met a Malik deputy.
The monitors have been unable to visit Kabul because of the fighting.
